To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
high-dose alpha-tocopherole (alpha-T) had no effect on the ethanol-induced pathological liver damage.
alpha-T supplementation did not prevent ethanol-induced liver damage in the intragastral feeding model.
high-dose vitamin E has no protective effect on chronic ethanol-induced liver injury.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of alpha-tocopheryl acetate (vitamin E, VE) on lipid peroxidation and ethanol-induced liver damage in the rat.
the effect of alpha-T on ethanol-induced liver injury.
the role of lipid peroxidation in the pathogenesis of alcoholic liver disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
in this rat model of ethanol-induced liver injury, vitamin E supplementation had no effect.
in the intragastic feeding rat model of chronic ethanol feeding, high-dose vitamin E has no effect on the development of liver damage and lipid peroxidation.
the effect of alpha-T supplementation on ethanol-induced pathological damage is dependent on the route of ethanol administration.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the protective effect of vitamin E against ethanol-induced liver damage is dependent on the route and duration of ethanol administration and the level of vitamin E supplementation.

the intragastrically administered ethanol model may not be a suitable model for studying the effect of antioxidants on alcohol-induced liver damage.
